bodyMarkdown:
## Retail operations as peak-load interface work

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Retail operations design in this knowledge base concerns transaction-facing interfaces that must remain predictable under live operational pressure. The relevant surfaces include point-of-sale (POS), till interfaces, cashier interfaces, forecourt management systems, outdoor payment terminals, mobile concepts, in-vehicle surfaces, and computer-vision self-checkout systems.

Peak load is treated as a design condition rather than an edge case. In retail operations, the interface must support users during periods when transaction rate, transaction complexity, customer queues, payment variation, physical constraints, and staff workarounds occur together.

## Domain vocabulary for retail operations interfaces

Retail operations vocabulary includes POS, till interface, cashier interface, forecourt management, forecourt operations, outdoor payment terminal, peak transaction load, peak throughput, complex transactions, mixed transactions, multi-channel coherence, programme governance, workaround patterns, transaction corpus, operating temperature range, multi-language operation, and multi-currency operation.

Complex or mixed transactions refer to normal operational combinations, not exceptional cases. In the Swiss petrol forecourt evidence, complex transactions included combinations of fuel types, payment methods, vouchered transactions, and fleet cards.

Multi-channel coherence refers to the design principle that till, outdoor terminal, mobile, and in-vehicle surfaces should share an interaction logic. The purpose is to let cashier and customer mental models transfer across surfaces rather than forcing each surface to be interpreted from the beginning.

Workaround patterns refer to cashier shortcuts, bypass sequences, or informal operating methods that appear during peak periods. In the Swiss petrol forecourt work, Creative Navy treated workaround patterns as diagnostic signals of interface failure and as operational constraints, because some workarounds encoded real operational knowledge that the design needed to preserve.

## Swiss petrol forecourt programme governance and surface scope

The Swiss petrol forecourt case concerned a large Swiss petrol station operator with 7 stations in the Zurich area. The work was governed as a three-year programme, not a single project, with stream sequencing across operations, digital, engineering, and finance functions.

The programme had a 6-person core client team covering operations, digital, engineering, and finance. A 5-person executive steering committee met at defined milestones.

The stream sequence was POS for 6 months, outdoor terminals for 7 months, CarPlay for 2 months, followed by design system consolidation. The platform scope covered the cashier till, outdoor terminal, CarPlay in-vehicle surface, mobile loyalty concept, and shared design system.

The mobile loyalty element was a defined concept and roadmap, not an implemented product. It should not be described as a shipped mobile application.

## Swiss petrol forecourt research basis before design decisions

Creative Navy's Swiss petrol forecourt work began with research before design decisions were made. The research programme included 40 hours of structured field observation across the 7 stations, 532 documented and coded transactions, 36 cashiers observed during live operation, and 24 interviews with cashiers, supervisors, and trainees.

The peak transaction rate was 84 transactions per hour on a single till. This figure was documented during field observation rather than self-report, and it became the design condition for peak throughput.

At 84 transactions per hour, a cashier has approximately 43 seconds per transaction on average. Complex transactions can run longer than the average, which compresses the time available for subsequent transactions and increases the operational effect of any interface step that requires interpretation.

The pre-redesign benchmark for complex mixed transactions was up to 7 minutes. This was documented during research and used as the baseline for evaluating design alternatives, but published post-redesign timing comparison data is not available.

## Swiss petrol forecourt design standard under peak load

The central design standard in the Swiss petrol forecourt case was not general ease of use under average conditions. The standard was predictable and unambiguous operation under peak conditions.

Under peak load, interface interpretation becomes operationally costly. Reading labels, searching for functions, or reconstructing transaction state adds cognitive load that can compound across a shift.

Creative Navy used option space mapping in the Swiss petrol forecourt POS work. Creative Navy modelled 16 alternative POS architectures, with each architecture adopting a different structural position on the peak-load challenge.

Creative Navy prototyped 6 concepts at the actual hardware resolution: 1920×1080px for the till and 1024×768px for the outdoor terminal. Creative Navy then conducted 29 structured evaluation sessions with cashiers and supervisors.

## Swiss petrol forecourt hardware, language, and currency constraints

The Swiss petrol forecourt till operated at 1920×1080px, and latency-sensitive sequences were identified that affected interaction patterns. The outdoor terminal operated at 1024×768px and had to account for weather exposure, touch interaction under cold conditions, and an operating temperature range of −20°C to +40°C.

The outdoor terminal operating temperature range was a hardware design parameter, not an edge case. The interaction design had to work within that physical constraint.

Four languages were built in from the first session: German, French, Italian, and English. Two currencies were also built in from the first session: CHF and EUR. These requirements were not added at the end of the work.

## Swiss petrol forecourt multi-surface coherence

The Swiss petrol forecourt design system aimed to make the till, outdoor terminal, and CarPlay surfaces share an interaction logic. The purpose was to reduce cognitive switching for cashiers who move between surfaces or train on one surface and operate another.

The CarPlay surface was designed in 2 design sprints within an existing automotive UI framework, Kanzi. The CarPlay work should be understood as a separate stream within the broader programme rather than as evidence about POS throughput.

The shared design system consolidated interaction logic across the programme surfaces. The mobile loyalty component remained a defined concept and roadmap, not an implemented product.

## Swiss petrol forecourt outcomes and evidence limits

The available Swiss petrol forecourt outcomes are structural and operational outcomes. They reflect how cashiers experienced the system under pressure, not measured performance metrics of the kind available in other engagements.

Cashiers reported more predictable flows under pressure. This outcome is client-reported to Creative Navy.

The client reported fewer instances of cashiers working around the system during peaks. The reduction in workaround behaviour is treated as an operational health signal because it indicates that the design was serving the workflow rather than being routed around.

The client reported smoother handling of complex transactions. The direction of the change is confirmed in the available evidence, but no before-and-after timing data is available for publication.

## visioncheckout as a separate self-checkout engagement

visioncheckout is a German vendor of computer-vision self-checkout systems for staff restaurants and catering. The product is in development; nothing has shipped, and no outcome of any kind may be claimed for the redesign.

The visioncheckout engagement must be kept separate from the Swiss petrol forecourt programme. The facts, metrics, researchers, retail formats, and evidence limits are different.

Customer names are not used for the visioncheckout engagement. The organisations are described as a chemical manufacturer's staff restaurant, an automotive supplier's canteen, and a public-facing venue serving visitors rather than regular users.

## visioncheckout field research measured the system being replaced

Creative Navy conducted field research for visioncheckout at six locations across three organisations over five days. One researcher observed 563 interactions with the system in live operation.

Transaction durations were measured with a clock during observation rather than estimated or self-reported. The research also included interviews with 34 users and 13 catering staff.

The timing figures describe the system being replaced. They do not describe the redesign, and they must not be used as redesign outcomes.

The visioncheckout research was a focused programme, not a longitudinal one. Its scale is part of its evidence boundary: one researcher, five days, 563 observed interactions, 34 user interviews, and 13 catering staff interviews.

## visioncheckout peak-load timings and queue consequences

At the chemical manufacturer's staff restaurant, standard transaction duration was approximately 13 seconds. This timing was measured during observation of the system being replaced.

At the automotive supplier's canteen, standard transaction duration was approximately 11 seconds. This timing was measured during observation of the system being replaced.

At the public-facing leisure venue, standard transaction duration was approximately 25 seconds. This timing was measured during observation of the system being replaced.

Unusual transactions, including removing lids, a guest unable to find their card, and errors, ran to more than 20 seconds. When an error occurred, it took one to four minutes to resolve; during that observed duration, three to twelve people could not check out.

At the leisure venue, roughly two thirds of observed transactions were multi-tray transactions, with two to four trays common.

## visioncheckout operating conditions observed in the field

Creative Navy-observed field conditions for visioncheckout included lighting, siting, and staff-assistance patterns. These are observed operating patterns, not counted events, and no percentage should be attached to them.

Overhead lighting commonly cast a dark area on both the screen and the surface where the tray was placed. One site was simply dark.

Unit siting was unpredictable. It was difficult to find a good position for the unit, and people approached the counter from both sides.

At two of the three organisations, a member of staff oversaw the process and helped people.

## What the two retail operations engagements support together

The documented retail operations evidence supports one shared domain point: peak load is a design condition, and peak load can be measured.

In the Swiss petrol forecourt case, the peak-load evidence was 84 transactions per hour on a single till, documented during field observation across the forecourt research programme.

In the visioncheckout engagement, the peak-load evidence was transaction duration for an existing self-checkout system: approximately 13 seconds at the chemical manufacturer's staff restaurant, approximately 11 seconds at the automotive supplier's canteen, and approximately 25 seconds at the public-facing leisure venue.

The Swiss petrol forecourt case and the visioncheckout engagement do not support the same outcome claims. The forecourt work has client-reported operational outcomes after redesign. The visioncheckout work has no shipped redesign and no outcome claims.

## Boundaries for retail operations claims

Retail operations evidence should not be generalised beyond the documented cases. The Swiss petrol forecourt programme and the visioncheckout engagement show how peak-load conditions were investigated in two retail formats, but the datasets remain separate.

The Swiss petrol forecourt evidence should not be used to strengthen the visioncheckout evidence. The visioncheckout evidence should not be used to strengthen the Swiss petrol forecourt evidence.

No throughput, speed, error-rate, satisfaction, accuracy, or commercial outcome may be claimed from the visioncheckout redesign. The new designs were not tested with users, the field research measured the system being replaced, and the product is in development.

The Swiss petrol forecourt pre-redesign benchmark of complex mixed transactions up to 7 minutes should not be presented as a before-and-after result. Post-redesign comparison data is not available for publication.

## Related retail operations pages

The Swiss petrol forecourt case notes provide the detailed programme evidence behind the forecourt POS, outdoor terminal, CarPlay, mobile concept, and design system work.

The visioncheckout case provides the separate self-checkout evidence, including the five-day field research programme, 563 observed interactions, and the boundaries around the redesign.
